ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adapting Language Models for Time Series Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task framework that fine-tunes a pre-trained language model to predict quality scores for time series data across diverse domains. The model will be trained on a dataset of labeled time series samples, where each sample is paired with a quality score based on domain-agnostic criteria (e.g., density, continuity). We will use the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as our primary metric to evaluate model performance, comparing our method against the state-of-the-art time series quality estimation methods, such as TimeInf and TimeShap.
CONTROLS: We will conduct ablation tests to evaluate the impact of different model architectures, fine-tuning strategies, and quality score criteria on model performance. Additionally, we will use a random baseline to assess the quality estimation capabilities of a language model without any fine-tuning.
COST: 1050
PREDICTION: We expect our model to outperform TimeInf and TimeShap in terms of MAE, especially in domains with complex time series patterns. However, it may struggle in domains with sparse or low-quality data, where the language model may not have enough contextual information to make accurate quality assessments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Language Models to Time Series Distribution Shifts
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a series of experiments to evaluate how well our multi-task framework adapts to different time series distribution shifts across the five experimental domains. We will use a set of pre-defined task-to-task transfer scenarios (e.g., from electricity load forecasting to exchange rate forecasting) to simulate distribution shifts and assess the effect of fine-tuning on model performance in these scenarios. We will use metrics such as accuracy and mean squared error to compare the robustness of our model to the baseline state-of-the-art methods.
CONTROLS: To identify the challenges posed by distribution shifts, we will analyze the performance of our model in a sequence of transfer scenarios, starting from the most similar tasks and increasingly moving to more dissimilar ones.
COST: 1850
PREDICTION: We expect our model to exhibit strong task-specific performance, reflecting the language model's transfer learning abilities. However, it may still suffer from substitution errors in the most dissimilar transfer scenarios, such as when switching from time series to non-time series tasks like handwriting recognition.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Quality Score Criteria on Language Model Performance
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an experiment to evaluate the impact of different quality score criteria on the performance of our multi-task framework. We will use a set of domain-agnostic quality score criteria, such as density, continuity, and smoothness, and compare the resulting model performance across these criteria. We will use the Mean Squared Error (MSE) metric to evaluate model performance in this experiment.
CONTROLS: To investigate the interaction between quality score criteria and model performance, we will also analyze the variance in model performance observed across different training runs using different quality score criteria.
COST: 2800
PREDICTION: We expect the choice of quality score criteria to significantly impact model performance, with some criteria better suited to certain domains than others. For example, density may lead to better performance in time series with sparse or irregular sampling patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Interpretability of Language Model Predictions for Time Series Quality
PROPOSAL: We will develop a method to interpret the predictions made by our multi-task framework for time series quality, providing a visual representation of the key factors contributing to the predicted quality score. We will use a combination of attention analysis and partial dependence plots to identify which parts of the time series are driving the quality assessment. We will also conduct an error analysis to assess the agreement between the language model's quality predictions and human assessments.
CONTROLS: To evaluate the accuracy of our interpretation method, we will use a selection of user-labeled time series samples and compare the insights provided by our method against these human assessments.
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: We expect our interpretation method to capture the temporal dependencies and patterns that the language model uses to make quality assessments, providing a useful tool for data analysts and domain experts to understand and validate the quality predictions made by our framework. However, it may struggle to capture nuanced or subtle quality-related aspects that are not immediately apparent from the data.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Quality Score Criteria on Language Model Performance
PROPOSAL: We revise our experiment to deepen our understanding of the relationship between quality score criteria and language model performance. Specifically, we will: (1) cluster the quality score criteria into groups based on their semantic similarity, (2) evaluate model performance on each cluster, and (3) compare the results to identify the most effective group of quality score criteria for each domain.
CONTROLS: We will also include a null hypothesis test to validate whether the performance differences between clusters are statistically significant.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: We expect our clustering approach to reveal patterns in quality score criteria that are relevant to each time series domain, and identify the most effective type of quality score criteria for each specific use case. However, it may be challenging to define a meaningful clustering algorithm for quality score criteria that captures their nuanced differences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Performance of Language Models on Misspecified Quality Score Criteria
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an experiment to investigate how language models perform when the quality score criteria are misspecified or based on incorrect assumptions about the data. We will intentionally corrupt the quality score criteria used during training and evaluate the model's performance under these conditions. We will also compare the results to the baseline performance when using correctly specified quality score criteria.
CONTROLS: To better understand how the corruption affects the results, we will analyze the changes in model performance across different levels of corruption and compare them to the baseline results.
COST: 3500
PREDICTION: We expect the language model to degrade in performance as the corruption level increases, especially in domains where the quality score criteria are tightly coupled with the underlying time series patterns. However, it may be challenging to generalize the results across different types of corruption and identify robust patterns.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Language Models to Time Series Distribution Shifts
PROPOSAL: We revise our experiment to incorporate domain adaptation techniques to improve the model's performance on distribution-shifted tasks. Specifically, we will use a multi-task learning approach to jointly train the model on multiple domains, sharing knowledge across tasks. We will evaluate the robustness of the model using a set of transfer learning benchmarks and compare the results to the baseline model.
CONTROLS: We will also include a hyperparameter search to find the optimal learning rate, batch size, and number of epochs for the multi-task learning approach.
COST: 3800
PREDICTION: We expect the domain adaptation techniques to improve the model's performance on distribution-shifted tasks, reducing the accuracy gap compared to the baseline model. However, it may be challenging to identify the optimal hyperparameters for the multi-task learning approach that work well across all domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Performance of Language Models on Time Series with Different Sampling Rates
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an experiment to evaluate the performance of our language model on time series data with varying sampling rates. We will use a set of real-world datasets with different sampling rates and compare the model's performance across these datasets. We will use metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Squared Error (MSE) to evaluate model performance.
CONTROLS: To understand how the sampling rate affects the model's performance, we will also conduct an analysis of variance (ANOVA) to identify significant differences in model performance across different sampling rates.
COST: 4200
PREDICTION: We expect the model to be more sensitive to sampling rate in domains with complex time series patterns, such as weather forecasting, but to be more robust in domains with simpler patterns, such as traffic forecasting. However, it may be challenging to identify a general trend that applies to all domains, as the relationship between sampling rate and model performance may be task-specific.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Adapting Language Models for Time Series Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: We revise our initial experiment to use a more advanced fine-tuning strategy that adapts the language model's weights to the task of time series quality estimation, rather than using a simple multi-task learning approach. We will use a self-supervised learning approach that trains the model on a set of pretext tasks that are related to time series quality estimation, such as forecasting and anomaly detection.
CONTROLS: We will include a series of ablation studies to evaluate the effectiveness of each component of the fine-tuning strategy and to identify the most important features that contribute to the model's performance.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect the self-supervised learning approach to lead to better performance and more robustness on time series quality estimation tasks, especially in domains with complex patterns and relationships. However, it may be challenging to design pretext tasks that are effective and generalizable across all domains, and to tune the weights of the language model to the task at hand.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Multi-Domain Study of Language Models for Time Series Quality Estimation
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a comprehensive study to evaluate the performance of language models for time series quality estimation across multiple domains, including electricity load forecasting, exchange rate forecasting, traffic forecasting, weather forecasting, handwriting recognition, and spacecraft telemetry anomaly detection. We will use a set of pre-defined quality score criteria and fine-tuning strategies to adapt the language model to each domain, and evaluate the model's performance using a range of metrics, including Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Squared Error (MSE).
CONTROLS: To identify the most effective approaches and gain insights into the relationships between domain, quality score criteria, and fine-tuning strategy, we will also conduct a series of ablation studies and analyze the results across different domains.
COST: 6600
PREDICTION: We expect the language model to demonstrate its ability to generalize across different domains, adapting to the specific needs and characteristics of each domain. However, it may be challenging to identify a single set of hyperparameters that works well across all domains, and to perform equally well on all quality score criteria.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pre-train+FT Baseline for Small Models
PROPOSAL: Compare the effectiveness of small language models pre-trained on synthetic data for text anonymization against models fine-tuned from a publicly available, smaller version of GPT-4. Both models will be evaluated on a suite of private attribute inference benchmarks, using a mix of strong LLM adversaries as extracting models. Model outputs will be anonymized and retained to prevent decoding, with metrics focusing on privacy loss (success rate of adversaries) and anonymized readability (distances to clean text).
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: large GPT-4 anonymizer/adversary pair (Proposed by subclasses of related work); (2) Ablation: removing pre-training step, or training on public rather than synthetic data; (3) Control group: adversarial training without fine-tuning or pre-training.
COST: 15 GigaHours
PREDICTION: We expect sizable gaps in both of the Comparison Attributes (i.e. privacy loss vs. readability distance to clean text) between the pre-train+FT and the large GPT-4 adversary models, and small but somewhat sizable drops with Ablation and Control groups.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Attribute Inference Detection
PROPOSAL: Implement a hierarchical attribute inference detection framework for strong LLM adversaries, leveraging a two-stage model that (i) utilizes the context-aware contrastive loss from Turn 3 to identify coarse-grained attribute inferences, and (ii) applies a variant of an adversary-inference localization mechanism to pinpoint the exact text spans that enable these coarse-grained inferences.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: non-hierarchical inference detection; (2) Ablation: Not utilizing coarse-grained inference detection; (3) Control group: inference detection without localization.
COST: 30 GigaHours
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical framework to significantly reduce the precision and recall of strong LLM adversaries in detecting private attribute inferences, and the localization mechanism to provide a more nuanced understanding of how text is exploited for inference.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Hierarchical Attribute Inference Detection
PROPOSAL: Implement a hierarchical attribute inference detection framework for strong LLM adversaries, leveraging a two-stage model that (i) utilizes the context-aware contrastive loss from Turn 3 to identify coarse-grained attribute inferences, and (ii) employs a dictionary-based method to pinpoint the exact text spans that enable these coarse-grained inferences, allowing for scalable inference detection.

CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: non-hierarchical inference detection; (2) Ablation: Not utilizing coarse-grained inference detection; (3) Control group: inference detection without dictionary-based localization.

COST: 32 GigaHours
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical framework to significantly reduce the precision and recall of strong LLM adversaries in detecting private attribute inferences, and the dictionary-based localization to provide accurate and efficient identification of text spans enabling inferences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Text Sanitization using Attention Decoupling
PROPOSAL: Introduce an attention decoupling technique for text sanitization, aiming to suppress sensitive information while preserving the original context and meaning. This approach modifies the attention mechanism within a small language model to selectively ignore certain words or tokens while aggregating the information from others, promoting the desired balance between preserving readability and protecting private information.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: basic text anonymization techniques; (2) Ablation: removing selective attention mechanism; (3) Control group: standard language model without sanitization.
COST: 40 GigaHours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the attention decoupling technique will help reduce the effectiveness of strong LLM adversaries in detecting private attribute inferences, while maintaining the clarity and coherence of sanitized text, and the sanitization rate to be at least 10-15%.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training with Constraint Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a constraint learning framework to guide the adversarial training process of strong LLM adversaries, with the goal of creating a more challenging and realistic inference environment for small models. This framework will impose constraints on the adversary's predictions to focus on specific private attributes or to emulate real-world inference scenarios, pushing the boundaries of small model anonymization capabilities.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard adversarial training; (2) Ablation: removing constraint learning; (3) Control group: weak LLM adversaries.
COST: 50 GigaHours
PREDICTION: We expect the constrained adversarial training to significantly increase the difficulty of inference detection for small models, achieving at least a 20-30% enhancement in adversary successes rates over our previous best anonymizer methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Local Model Adaptation for Text Anonymization
PROPOSAL: Propose a local model adaptation mechanism that allows small models to adapt to specific domains or text styles during inference, enhancing their anonymization capabilities in settings with distinct contextual requirements. This approach will leverage a domain-invariant adaptation module to adjust the model's output based on the input text's characteristics, enabling more effective protection of private information in diverse scenarios.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard small model anonymization; (2) Ablation: removing domain-invariant adaptation module; (3) Control group: large models with domain adaptation.
COST: 60 GigaHours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the local model adaptation mechanism will lead to a 15-20% improvement in anonymization effectiveness in challenging domain-specific scenarios, while maintaining a competitive level of performance in general setting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model Robustness and Adversarial Vulnerability
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the robustness and adversarial vulnerability of small models in text anonymization scenarios, considering both inference attacks and model manipulation. This framework will include metrics to measure model resilience, attack success rates, and the impact of adversarial training on model stability, providing a deeper understanding of small model performance under different threat scenarios.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: standard evaluation metrics; (2) Ablation: removing model manipulation assessment; (3) Control group: large models with robustness evaluation.
COST: 80 GigaHours
PREDICTION: We expect the comprehensive evaluation framework to reveal significant differences in the robustness of small models to inference attacks and model manipulation, highlighting the need for more robust and adaptive anonymization strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable and Privacy-Friendly Text Anonymization Pipeline
PROPOSAL: Design and implement a scalable and privacy-friendly text anonymization pipeline that integrates the techniques developed throughout this research, enabling efficient and effective protection of private information in large-scale text datasets. This pipeline will leverage a combination of pre-processing, anonymization, and post-processing stages to ensure high-quality anonymization outcomes while maintaining performance and efficiency.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: current state-of-the-art text anonymization techniques; (2) Ablation: removing individual anonymization stages; (3) Control group: large models with centralized anonymization.
COST: 100 GigaHours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the scalable and privacy-friendly text anonymization pipeline will achieve a significant reduction in private information exposure, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques by at least 20-30% in terms of anonymity and readability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Establishing Non-Asymptotic Sample-Complexity Bounds for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We aim to prove non-asymptotic sample-complexity guarantees for KernelSHAP using a concentration inequality on the weighted least-squares objective. Specifically, we will utilize a Hanson-Wright inequality for the Frobenius norm of the matrix product between the sub-sampled kernel weights and the design matrix, adapted to the weighted least-squares framework used in KernelSHAP. We will leverage this result to derive high-probability bounds on the reconstruction error between the full-sample and sub-sampled Shapley values, providing a sample complexity guarantee for KernelSHAP.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Jensen-Shannon divergence between full-sample and sub-sampled Shapley values; Abations: none
COST: 20000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We hope to achieve a sample-complexity guarantee of O(1/ε) to achieve accuracy ε in the Shapley values, albeit in potentially a more conservative regime compared to the practical performance of KernelSHAP. The derivation could fail to be tight, or fail to encompass the implicit regularization effects that improve KernelSHAP's performance in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extension of Sample-Complexity Bounds to Unbiased KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We extend our previous result on non-asymptotic sample-complexity bounds for KernelSHAP to Unbiased KernelSHAP, the unbiased variant with asymptotic variance analysis. We achieve this by analyzing the additional variance introduced by the reweighting and sub-sampling scheme in Unbiased KernelSHAP, and then incorporating this variance into our concentration inequality framework. Like before, we leverage the Hanson-Wright inequality and adapt it to the weighted least-squares objective with reweighted and sub-sampled data.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Sample complexity guarantee for KernelSHAP from Proposal 1; Abations: Different sample schemes, reweighting strategies
COST: 35000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the sample-complexity guarantee for Unbiased KernelSHAP to be higher than that of KernelSHAP, possibly scaling like O(1/ε^2) to achieve accuracy ε in the Shapley values. However, Unbiased KernelSHAP's performance in practice has been observed to underperform the original KernelSHAP, so it is unclear whether this theoretical expectation holds in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Leverage-Based Sample-Complexity Bounds for LeverageSHAP
PROPOSAL: We derive non-asymptotic sample-complexity bounds for LeverageSHAP, the regression-based estimator that samples rows according to their statistical leverage scores. We analyze the concentration of the weighted least-squares objective in LeverageSHAP's sampling scheme, using a combination of the Hanson-Wright inequality and the properties of statistical leverage scores. Our result provides a sample complexity guarantee for LeverageSHAP, vital for understanding its performance in practice.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Sample complexity guarantee for KernelSHAP from Proposal 1; Abations: Different sampling schemes for statistical leverage scores, Regularization
COST: 40000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that LeverageSHAP's sample-complexity guarantee will be tighter than that of KernelSHAP, with a scaling potentially as low as O(1/ε) to achieve accuracy ε in the Shapley values. However, the proof may become increasingly technical and difficult to work with, especially when incorporating the properties of statistical leverage scores.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Improved Analytical Bounds for LeverageSHAP
PROPOSAL: We refine the analysis of LeverageSHAP's concentration by incorporating more precise analytical bounds on the statistical leverage scores and their impact on the sampling scheme. This involves leveraging recent advances in eigenvalue concentration inequalities to derive sharper bounds on the matrix product between the sub-sampled kernel weights and the design matrix. As a result, we improve LeverageSHAP's sample-complexity guarantee, providing a tighter bound on the reconstruction error between the full-sample and sub-sampled Shapley values.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Revised sample complexity guarantee for KernelSHAP from Proposal 1; Abations: Different analytical bounds for statistical leverage scores, Regularization
COST: 42000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the improved analytical bounds will lead to a significant reduction in the sample complexity required to achieve accuracy ε in the Shapley values, potentially even better than O(1/ε). However, refining these bounds may become increasingly cumbersome and our derivation may become challenging to verify.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: SimSHAP's Computational Tractability for High-Dimensional Data
PROPOSAL: We analyze SimSHAP, a recently proposed parametric approach to computing Shapley values for high-dimensional data, and establish its computational tractability. We show that SimSHAP can efficiently compute Shapley values even in high-dimensional settings by leveraging the properties of the parametric model and the manifold structure of the input data. Our result highlights SimSHAP as a promising approach for scaling Shapley value computations to large datasets.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Computational time for existing high-dimensional Shapley value methods (e.g., LIME); Abations: Different parametric models, manifold learning techniques
COST: 55000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect SimSHAP to exhibit a spectacular reduction in computational time compared to traditional Shapley value methods for high-dimensional data, since it inherits the benefits of manifold learning and leverage score-based sampling. However, it remains unclear how well SimSHAP will generalize to data with complex, non-linear relationships between features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: An Empirical Comparison of KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP, and SimSHAP
PROPOSAL: We conduct a thorough empirical comparison of the performance of three prominent Shapley value estimators: KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP, and SimSHAP. We assess their accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency across various datasets and models from the literature, including linear, non-linear, and high-dimensional settings. Our goal is to yield a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each estimator in different scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Each estimator's accuracy and running time individually; Abations: Different evaluation metrics, Dataset and model selection
COST: 75000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the experimental results to reveal: (i) the dominance of LeverageSHAP and SimSHAP over KernelSHAP for high-dimensional data and non-linear relationships, respectively; (ii) the trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency among estimators; (iii) instances where one estimator excels, yet others fail to provide reliable explanations. However, replicating such wide-ranging experiments may become computationally expensive and requires careful dataset curation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Global Sensitivity Analysis using Shapley Values for Real-World Applications
PROPOSAL: We demonstrate the utility of Shapley values for global sensitivity analysis in real-world applications, focusing on finance and healthcare domains. We develop novel algorithms to efficiently compute Shapley values on large datasets and present case studies on risk assessment and patient stratification tasks. Our work highlights the practical potential of Shapley values for quantifying variable importance and coping with uncertainty in actionable ways.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Traditional global sensitivity analysis methods (e.g., variance-based sensitivity analysis); Abations: Different post-processing techniques, Models and data from other domains
COST: 95000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate significant interest in global sensitivity analysis based on Shapley values due to their interpretability and quantitative reliability, while also acknowledging potential scalability challenges in data-rich settings. Our methods may uncover new layers of variable importance not detected by prior methods, though this will depend on the effectiveness of the Shapley values computations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theory and Practice of Sub-Sampling for Model-Agnostic Interpretability
PROPOSAL: We bridge the gap between theory and practice of sub-sampling for model-agnostic interpretability by developing a theoretical framework to analyze the implicit regularization effects of sub-sampling on Shapley value estimation. Building on our previous work on sample-complexity bounds, we extend the analysis to non-uniform sub-sampling schemes and leverage the results to improve the efficiency and accuracy of estimators like KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Current theoretical frameworks for sub-sampling (e.g., concentration inequalities); Abations: Different sub-sampling schemes, Model-agnostic interpretability techniques
COST: 110000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the new theoretical framework to enable more efficient and robust Shapley value estimations, particularly for complex models and large datasets, while also expanding our understanding of the interplay between sub-sampling, regularization, and interpretability. Challenges may arise in proving the generalizability of our findings and adapting the methods to emerging model-agnostic interpretability techniques.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Enhanced Concentration Inequalities for Shapley Value Estimation
PROPOSAL: We revisit the concentration inequality in Proposal 1 and enhance it using a more refined concentration measure that accounts for the specific structure of the Shapley value estimation problem. This involves leveraging recent advances in matrix concentration and eigenvalue-based inequalities to derive sharper concentration bounds. As a result, we obtain tighter sample-complexity guarantees for KernelSHAP and its variants.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Revised sample complexity guarantee for KernelSHAP from Proposal 1; Abations: Different concentration measures, Regularization techniques
COST: 120000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The refined concentration inequality is expected to yield significant improvements in the sample complexity bounds for Shapley value estimation, potentially reducing the required sample size by orders of magnitude. However, the enhanced inequality may introduce additional technical difficulties and require more sophisticated proof techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Unified Framework for Model-Agnostic Interpretability: Shapley Values and Beyond
PROPOSAL: We develop a comprehensive framework for model-agnostic interpretability that unifies and generalizes existing methods, including Shapley values, feature importance, and partial dependence plots. Our framework leverages theoretical foundations from game theory, economic theory, and statistics to derive novel bounds and guarantees for these methods. We also extend our framework to novel applications, such as fair regression and causal inference.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Current state-of-the-art methods for model-agnostic interpretability (e.g., SHAP, LIME); Abations: Different frameworks, Theoretical foundations
COST: 150000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unified framework is expected to provide a principled and rigorous approach to model-agnostic interpretability, yielding improved accuracy, robustness, and explainability for a wide range of applications. However, the framework's generality and flexibility may require significant additional proof and verification efforts to ensure its correctness and applicability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bridging Branched Trajectories with Stochastic Processes
PROPOSAL: We formulate the Stochastic Process Bridge (SPB), an extension of the Schrödinger bridge problem that enables modeling branched trajectories between a pair of endpoint distributions. We define a balance equation for the total mass over time, accounting for birth and death events as branches diverge and merge, and learn a drift field and a set of stochastic processes that minimize the Kullback-Leibler divergence to an underlying reference process. The SPB is trained on real-world cell differentiation and drug perturbation response data, and evaluated on various branching metrics and trajectory reconstruction tasks.
CONTROLS: Schrödinger bridge matching, generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations
COST: 45.6
PREDICTION: SPB will outperform existing methods in modeling branched trajectories, but may fail to accurately capture long-term branch merging or growth dynamics due to the challenges of learning complex temporal relationships and mass redistribution patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Stochastic Process Bridge with Temporal Aggregation
PROPOSAL: We extend the Stochastic Process Bridge (SPB) to dynamically aggregate branching events over short time horizons, enabling the model to learn the timing and rate of mass redistribution between branches while preserving the overall branched structure of the trajectory. Temporal aggregation is achieved through a novel smoothing spline-based approximation of the mass balance equation over aggregated time intervals, which modifies the SPB loss function to encourage smoother and more consistent mass flows between branches.
CONTROLS: SPB (baseline), generalized Schrödinger bridge formulations (ablation for no temporal aggregation)
COST: 36.9
PREDICTION: Temporal aggregation will significantly improve the SPB's ability to capture branching events and mass redistribution patterns, but may introduce artifacts in cases where the branching dynamics exhibit rapid and high-frequency variations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph-Based Branching Representation Learning (GBRL)
PROPOSAL: We develop the Graph-Based Branching Representation Learning (GBRL) framework, which represents branched trajectories as an attributed graph, where each node corresponds to a short-term sampling from the underlying stochastic process, and edges capture the flow of mass between consecutive sampling times. To leverage this graph representation, we introduce a novel branch-and-matching loss that matching GBRL graphs to the branching patterns in the target distribution, which is learned through a contrastive learning objective.
CONTROLS: SPB (baseline), Schrödinger bridge matching (ablation for no graph representation)
COST: 39.3
PREDICTION: GBRL will provide a powerful representation for modeling branched trajectories, capturing both the spatial structure and temporal dynamics of the branching events, but its computational complexity may become a limiting factor for large-scale applications.

ACTION: REVISE 3
 TITLE: Graph-Based Branching Representation Learning (GBRL)
PROPOSAL: We revise GBRL to incorporate a separate graph attention mechanism that selectively focuses on the most informative edges connecting branches, thereby pruning away noisy or irrelevant connections and improving the overall representation of branched trajectories. This attention-based graph refinement enhances the contrastive learning objective of GBRL, allowing it to better match the branching patterns in the target distribution.

TITLE: Frequency-Aware Bias Control for Weight Matrix Updates in PEFT
PROPOSAL: When applying PEFT methods like LoRA or the prior-guess layer to LOMs, it is essential to prevent the projected weight updates from biased towards certain frequencies, potentially compromising the model's ability to generalize across the PDE's solution manifold. We propose Frequency-Aware Bias Control (FABC), a simple yet effective framework for adjusting weight matrix updates to ensure that the frequency components of the learned weights remain representative of the pre-trained model's spectral knowledge. In FABC, we introduce a bias term that depends on the frequency content of the projected updates and is adjusted based on the similarity between the pre-trained and fine-tuned models' spectral representations. We will test FABC in combination with SiGN and LoRA on the synthetic datasets for Navier-Stokes, shallow-water, and solar magnetohydrodynamics simulations.
CONTROLS: We will compare the generalization performance of FABC-enabled PEFT approaches against the standard LoRA and prior-guess layer methods, as well as their combinations with SiGN.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: We expect FABC to significantly improve the generalization performance of PEFT methods for LOMs in SciML by preventing biased frequency components in the projected weight updates, and to synergistically enhance the efficacy of SiGN when combined.

PROPOSAL: To further enhance the robustness of PEFT methods for LOMs, we propose Task-Conditional Sampling (TCS), a spectral-sampling approach that adapts the sampling distribution to the specific task at hand. TCS is based on the idea of conditioning the frequency samples on the task loss and spectral representations of both the pre-trained and fine-tuned models. This approach allows for more efficient exploration of the task-relevant frequency components, improving the model's ability to generalize to new PDEs. We will evaluate TCS in combination with SiGN, LoRA, and the prior-guess layer on the synthetic datasets for various PDE types and compare its performance against standard fine-tuning.

PROPOSAL: We wish to extend the infinite-width limit analysis of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) to deep ReLU networks, establishing a closed-form expression for the NTK Gram matrix. This would allow us to derive explicit risk bounds and understand the impact of depth on the NTK. Specifically, we aim to generalize the existing result for two-layer ReLU networks to deeper architectures. We will use the framework of [Colombo et al., 2020] and leverage the recent advances on the NTK for ReLU networks [Arora et al., 2019].

ACTION: ADD #2
TITLE: Stability Analysis for Deep ReLU Networks via Bounded Hessian Norm
PROPOSAL: We aim to develop a stability analysis for deep ReLU networks, leveraging recent advances on the bounded Hessian norm [Araya et al., 2022]. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lightweight Vector Aggregation for Hybrid Multimodal Retrieval
PROPOSAL: We propose a new lightweight and architecture-agnostic vector aggregation method for combining the outputs of heterogeneous retrievers. Given two vectors u and v from different retrievers, we compute their weighted mean along the embedding dimension, but also take into account their cosine similarity to prevent dimensionality mismatch. The aggregation weight is calculated using the neuron similarity between the retrievers' common layers, which shares information on the learnable parameters and the model architecture.  
CONTROLS: Simple Mean (SM) and Weighted Mean (WM) aggregation as baselines. For ablation, we consider using fixed weights instead of dynamically computed weights.  
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to achieve better results than simple mean aggregation, while avoiding the computationally expensive weights calculation. However, if the neuron similarity calculation fails to capture the model's architecture, the method may not perform significantly better than WM aggregation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hybrid Retrieval for Visual Document Retrieval using ColPali
PROPOSAL: We conduct experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of hybrid retrieval in the context of visual document retrieval, combining a ColPali-based multimodal retriever with a dense text retriever using BM25 as a baseline. We also evaluate the performance of our previously proposed Lightweight Vector Aggregation method in enhancing the ColPali/BM25 hybrid retriever configuration.  
CONTROLS: ColPali alone, BM25 alone, ColPali+Bov-GST (another state-of-the-art multimodal retriever). For ablation, we consider replacing the BM25 baseline with a more sophisticated text retriever, such as an Oracle or compressed semantic search model.  
COST: 4900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the ColPali/BM25 hybrid retriever to achieve strong performance on visual document retrieval benchmarks, given the complementary strengths of text and image encodings. However, the performance gain may not be substantial, and the hybrid retriever might require careful tuning of weights and model parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Heterogeneous Dimensionality on Vector Aggregation
PROPOSAL: We explore the performance of Lightweight Vector Aggregation under different scenarios of heterogeneous dimensionality between the two retrievers. We evaluate the effect of dimensionality mismatch by sampling the ColPali vectors to match the dimensionality of the BM25 vectors, and compare the performance with the original vectors and the ones with randomly projected lower dimensionality.  
CONTROLS: Dimensionality-matched vectors with no modification, and randomly projected lower dimensionality vectors.  
COST: 1170 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that vector aggregation will perform poorly when vectors are significantly mismatched in dimensionality, but will achieve better results when the vectors are either dimensionality-matched or one set of vectors is randomly projected to a lower dimensionality. However, if the lightweight text retriever produces vectors with an extremely low dimensionality, vector aggregation might fail to capture the retriever's signal, leading to poor performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ablating the Neuron Similarity Calculation in Lightweight Vector Aggregation
PROPOSAL: We examine the importance of the neuron similarity calculation in Lightweight Vector Aggregation by replacing it with three alternative methods: Cosine Similarity, Euclidean Distance, and-static Weights. We compare the performance of these ablated methods against the full Lightweight Vector Aggregation approach and the baseline Weighted Mean aggregation.  
CONTROLS: Ablated methods using Cosine Similarity, Euclidean Distance, and static Weights instead of neuron similarity.  
COST: 2010 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that the original Lightweight Vector Aggregation method using neuron similarity will outperform the ablated methods, as it leverages learnable parameters and model architecture to compute the aggregation weight. However, if the neuron similarity calculation fails, the Cosine Similarity or Euclidean Distance-based methods might provide a good alternative, or even the simple Weighted Mean aggregation, suggesting that Lightweight Vector Aggregation might be more robust than initially expected.

PROPOSAL: We propose a novel unsupervised point cloud denoising method, titled 'GeoDiff', which utilizes a geodesic diffusion process to smoothen the noisy point cloud. The approach involves embedding the points into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and then conducting a biased stochastic regularization process to diffuse the noise. TITLE: Evaluating Inter-Modal Catastrophic Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Generative Models
PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to compare the performance of UMGMs before and after task switching, measuring inter-modal forgetting by evaluating the pre-trained image generation ability after fine-tuning on a sequence of multimodal understanding tasks. We select a state-of-the-art UMGM (DALL-E 3) and our target tasks: VQAv2 (visual question answering) and i2icl (image-to-image conditional likelihood dataset for text-to-image generation). We evaluate this UMGM on both tasks using the accuracy metric for VQAv2 and inception score for i2icl. To quantify inter-modal forgetting, we also calculate the difference in inception score between the pre-trained model and the model fine-tuned on VQAv2, as a proxy for forgetting of visual generation capabilities.

TITLE: Bayesian Adversarial Training for Probabilistic Supervision
PROPOSAL: We propose a theoretical framework, Bayesian Adversarial Training (BAT), to analyze the effect of probabilistic supervision on the convergence and generalization of SGD-based learning. Given a teacher model that provides an estimated class posterior probability distribution P(Y|x) over the classes Y for a given input x, we add an adversarial noise term to the student's objective function to regularize its optimization trajectory. Specifically, we construct an adversarial loss that acts as an upper bound on the data-dependent term in the student's expected risk.
L_adv = H(P || Q), where P and Q are the true and estimated posterior distributions, and H denotes the Kullback-Leibler divergence. We integrate this adversarial loss into the standard SGD update rule and theoretically analyze its convergence properties, providing new insights into the impact of probabilistic supervision on SGD-based learning.

TITLE: Sharp Risk Bounds for Probabilistic Distillation Under MMD-based Regularization
PROPOSAL: We establish sharp excess-risk bounds for probabilistic distillation under maximum mean discrepancy (MMD)-based regularization, a common choice of regularization technique in knowledge distillation. Given a teacher model T that estimates a posterior probability distribution P_T, we consider a student model S trained with an objective incorporating both cross-entropy and MMD terms, weighting the teacher's outputs: F = CE(S, P_T) + λMMD(S, P_T). We derive a data-dependent term of the excess risk bound in terms of the distance between the teacher's and student's predictions, leveraging the MMD to quantify the quality of the teacher's estimations. We bound this distance further, leading to an excess-risk bound on the student's performance. Our analysis sheds light on the statistical benefits and the trade-off between precision and recall in probabilistic knowledge distillation under MMD regularization.

PROPOSAL: We investigate a novel approach to modifying stationary random Fourier features to adapt to local, input-dependent structure in non-stationary kernels. ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Non-Linear Attention Mixture
PROPOSAL: We investigate the Residual Channel Attention mechanism, which extends the standard attention read by predicting channel-wise mixing weights for a non-linear mixture of past values. Specifically, for each query $q_t$, we predict a weight vector $w_t$ and apply it to the non-linearly transformed values $v_i$: $o_t=\sum_{i\le t}w_{t,i}\sigma(\alpha_{t,i}v_i+b)$, where $\sigma$ is an element-wise ReLU or Sigmoid function, and $b$ is a learned bias term. This allows channels to retrieve different past indices and attend to non-linearly transformed values in a single step.
CONTROLS: Standard softmax attention-based model, ablation models with different weight prediction mechanisms (e.g. simple linear weights, sparse attention) and signal transformations (e.g. no transformation, linear transformation)
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: Depending on the choice of weight prediction mechanism and signal transformation, we can significantly reduce the linear read bottleneck, enabling per-channel, context-dependent selection; however, training stability may suffer, particularly if the number of channels is large.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Adaptive Channel Projection
PROPOSAL: We propose using Adaptive Channel Projections (ACP) to selectively retrieve relevant past values for each channel. At each query step, ACP predicts a learnable projection matrix $P_t$ for each channel. This matrix is applied to the key values $K$, producing a channel-specific set of projected key values, which are then used to compute the attention scores. The final read is obtained by selecting the top-$k$ projected key values and mixing them using learnable weights. This approach enables each channel to selectively focus on relevant past indices, breaking the linear read bottleneck.
CONTROLS: ACP with different projection matrix prediction mechanisms (e.g. multi-layer perceptron, sparse attention) and selection strategies (e.g. top-$k$, sorted)
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: ACP can significantly improve performance on tasks requiring per-channel, context-dependent selection; however, the choice of projection matrix prediction mechanism and selection strategy greatly impacts performance, and over-selecting may lead to suboptimal results.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Interleaved Attention Networks
PROPOSAL: We design Interleaved Attention Networks (IAN), a hierarchical attention mechanism that resolves the linear read bottleneck. IAN consists of multiple interleaved attention layers, each processing a subset of channels. In each layer, the model predicts attention scores and weighs the corresponding values from previous layers, allowing for per-channel, context-dependent selection. The final read is obtained by concatenating the outputs of all layers. IAN enables the model to selectively focus on relevant past indices for each channel while maintaining causal parallelism.
CONTROLS: IAN with different interleaving strategies (e.g. depth-wise, channel-wise) and attention score prediction mechanisms (e.g. standard softmax, sparse attention)
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: IAN can overcome the linear read bottleneck and achieve state-of-the-art performance on tasks requiring per-channel, context-dependent selection; however, the choice of interleaving strategy and attention score prediction mechanism impacts performance, and over-complexity may lead to training instability.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Hierarchical Attention Jumping Learning
PROPOSAL: We introduce Hierarchical Attention Jumping Learning (HAJL), a method that enables the model to selectively jump to relevant past indices across different time steps. HAJL consists of a hierarchical attention mechanism that predicts attention scores for both spatial and temporal jumps. In each attention head, the model predicts two sets of weights: one for spatial attention and another for temporal jumping. The spatial weights are used to compute attention scores as in standard attention, while the temporal weights are used to jump to relevant past indices. The final read is obtained by concatenating the outputs of the spatial and temporal attention mechanisms. HAJL allows the model to capture long-range dependencies and correlations across different time steps.
CONTROLS: HAJL with different hierarchical attention mechanisms (e.g. standard hierarchical attention, adaptive hierarchical attention) and temporal weight prediction mechanisms (e.g. standard softmax, sparse attention)
COST: 6500
PREDICTION: HAJL can significantly improve performance on tasks requiring long-range modeling and selective attention, such as weather forecasting and electricity transformer load forecasting, by enabling the model to jump to relevant past indices and capture complex temporal correlations.
